description: "Somos un grupo de estudiantes riobambeñas de la UEISIL apasionadas por comprender el funcionamiento de nuestro planeta. A través de este proyecto, combinamos nuestras habilidades en arte, investigación, análisis de datos y creación de contenido multimedia. Con disciplina y determinación, buscamos generar un impacto real que nazca hoy y escale con el tiempo."
summary:
What did you develop?
We developed a 3D gallery interface that compiles information from NASA—specifically from the Earth Information Center (EIC)—to make it accessible and functional for people with visual impairments. Thanks to the UDL (Universal Design for Learning) methodology, we also expanded its usability to users with hearing impairments, neurodivergent individuals, or those who have difficulty retaining information.

How does it address the challenge?
We translate EIC data and imagery into an audio-based model. Each experience is adapted for blind individuals through identifiable soundscapes that represent both the selected visual content and its consequences in a real-world environment.

Why is it important?
Limiting this knowledge to a single standard user profile creates significant gaps. Making this information accessible allows everyone, regardless of their physical or social context, to understand how their own planet works.
details:
Our project is an immersive virtual museum that transforms data and images from NASA’s Earth Information Center (EIC) into multisensory experiences—incorporating sounds, narratives, visuals, and vibrations. It begins with an interactive welcome and a test that tailors the interface to the user’s specific needs, subsequently guiding them through a 360° space divided into three rooms (Water, Fire, and Air) featuring interactive sound, floor sensors, a real-time avatar, and a virtual assistant named Mini Gaia.

The benefits offered by our website stem from our application of Universal Design for Learning (UDL) and "anchor themes" that connect science to everyday situations. GAIA conveys information through multiple channels without overwhelming the senses. This enables adolescents and adults—including individuals with visual or hearing impairments, as well as neurodivergent people—to spark genuine curiosity, gain a better understanding, and learn at their own pace, utilizing the specialized resources previously mentioned.

The primary impact of GAIA is to ensure that individuals with visual impairments can explore and understand science, without their inability to see hindering their learning. In Ecuador, there are 270,000 people with visual impairments. Furthermore, a survey of young people revealed that most abandon the traditional EIC platform within seconds due to its complex language. By transforming NASA’s visual data into accessible sounds, narrations, and vibrations, the project aims to spark genuine curiosity, improve information retention, and expand educational opportunities for those currently excluded. Looking ahead, we plan to test the prototype with actual users to refine it and develop it into a mobile application.

The programming tools we used for our projects included HTML5 and Gemini, which were employed to develop the 3D architecture, lighting, real-time avatars, floor sensors, and the "Mini Gaia" assistant, as well as to integrate visual data from NASA’s EIC. Finally, we compressed the project into a .zip file and deployed it on AWS Amplify as a lightweight WebView, compatible with both computers and smartphones.

The creativity of our project lies in pushing beyond the boundaries of traditional science communication by transforming static data and images from NASA into interactive, multisensory experiences. Inspired by the Rijksmuseum’s "Masterpieces Up Close," GAIA breaks new ground by translating Earth’s phenomena into soundscapes and tactile vibrations—allowing users to "feel" and hear science without relying on sight—while incorporating "anchor themes" from everyday life to spark genuine curiosity.

Primarily, we consider various learning methods tailored to each user’s individual, physical, and social context—including blind, deaf, and neurodivergent individuals—by applying Universal Design for Learning (UDL) and an initial assessment that adapts the experience to the user’s own pace. Furthermore, drawing on John Sweller’s Cognitive Load Theory and our own surveys, we replace technical jargon with plain language; we prioritize a lightweight WebView architecture to ensure smooth performance on any mobile device; and we have assembled an interdisciplinary team that combines empathy, methodological research, and data analysis from NASA.
